intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From self-authorizing knight to reconciled Christian self
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Highly agentic self-assertion: he begins as a self-fashioning, mastery-seeking knight who imposes his will on reality, pursues fame, and treats others as supporting roles in his chivalric mission.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Communal, relationally embedded selfhood: he ends as Alonso Quixano, oriented toward confession, gratitude, family protection, and peaceful reconciliation with others and with God.

trajectory.position_description: He begins in maximal agency: he renames himself, arms himself, leaves home, recruits a squire, and insists on his own chivalric mission despite ridicule.
key_moments: Renames himself Don Quixote and Rocinante
Secures dubbing and begins sallying forth
Recruits Sancho Panza
Treats others as supporting roles in his quest

trajectory.position_description: Agency remains high but becomes increasingly mediated by others: he dominates interpretation, seeks public validation, and uses chivalric identity as a social performance while growing more dependent on Sancho and courtly audiences.
key_moments: Explains defeats as enchantment rather than error
Defends knight-errantry in long speeches
Advises Sancho on governance and conduct
Accepts courtly honors and public staging

trajectory.position_description: After defeat, his agency is sharply reduced and redirected inward: he submits to retirement, relinquishes the knightly self, and turns toward repentance, confession, and domestic responsibility.
key_moments: Defeated by the Knight of the White Moon
Returns home subdued and reflective
Makes his will and confesses
Renounces chivalric books and becomes Alonso Quixano the Good

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The arc moves from maximal self-assertion to a final state of humility, dependence, and relational repair. The middle of the novel preserves agency but increasingly socializes it, so the ending is best read as a genuine reorientation rather than a simple collapse.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From impermeable enchantment to lucid renunciation
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Fully enclosed in delusion: he treats romances as reality, misreads ordinary objects as enchanted signs, and explains contradiction through magic rather than self-correction.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Clear-eyed renunciation: he explicitly names his former madness, rejects chivalric books as harmful falsehoods, and recognizes his life as a moral error requiring repentance.

trajectory.position_description: He consistently converts the world into chivalric fantasy, with only tactical flexibility inside the delusion.
key_moments: Inn becomes castle
Windmills become giants
Defeats are explained as enchantment
Sierra Morena penance is treated as literal chivalric performance

trajectory.position_description: He remains deluded, but the delusion is increasingly staged, publicly manipulated, and occasionally tested by practical reality; he sometimes notices facts, but absorbs them back into enchantment.
key_moments: Courtly pranks and staged enchantments at the duke's castle
Cave of Montesinos and Clavileño intensify wonder without correction
He can occasionally distinguish local realities from fantasy
He preserves his worldview by reclassifying contradictions

trajectory.position_description: The delusional system collapses into explicit renunciation; he sees his former self as mad and rejects knight-errantry as deception.
key_moments: Defeat by the Knight of the White Moon
Melancholy retreat home
Confession and will-making
Renounces Don Quixote and becomes Alonso Quixano

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: This is the clearest psychological arc in the material: from complete enchantment-thinking to a final repudiation of that worldview. The middle chapters show resilient, adaptive delusion rather than true realism, making the ending a decisive break.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist
structuralist.reasoning: Published scholarship does support a late movement in Don Quixote from delusive chivalric self-enclosure toward lucid self-recognition and renunciation. Structural and narratological readings of the novel regularly treat the ending as a reversal in which the knight explicitly repudiates his books, names his madness, and reenters ordinary moral reality, even if critics differ on how complete or stable that lucidity is.

relational_axes.pole_start: He begins by recruiting Sancho as a subordinate squire, treating him as useful, persuadable, and intellectually inferior within the chivalric hierarchy.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This is the richest relationship arc in the novel: it moves from hierarchy to intimacy, from comic mismatch to genuine mutual attachment. Don Quixote never stops being the master, but by the end he is also deeply dependent on and emotionally attached to Sancho.

relational_axes.axis_name: From fantasized lady to final moral center
relational_axes.pole_start: She begins as a wholly fantasized courtly beloved, an abstract lady who legitimizes his knightly identity.
relational_axes.pole_end: She ends as the enduring moral and emotional center of his life, even as he renounces knight-errantry and repents.

trajectory.position_description: Dulcinea is the imagined source of his mission, honor, and courtly language; she is intensely idealized but not yet morally tested.
key_moments: Transforms Aldonza Lorenzo into Dulcinea
Invokes her in first combats
Uses her as the standard for all chivalric action

trajectory.position_description: She becomes the fixed center of his identity, the justification for penance, resistance to temptation, and all public self-presentation.
key_moments: Sierra Morena penance
Refusal of Altisidora
Dulcinea's disenchantment becomes the engine of the later plot
He repeatedly insists on her exclusivity and beauty

trajectory.position_description: Even as he renounces chivalry, Dulcinea remains the beloved whose memory structures his repentance and final moral order.
key_moments: Refuses to deny her beauty in the duel
Continues to seek her disenchantment after defeat
Dies as Alonso Quixano while still honoring her place in his life

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Dulcinea never becomes a real interpersonal relationship, but she becomes the deepest organizing attachment in his psyche. The arc is less about change in feeling than about increasing moral centrality, surviving even the collapse of his knightly identity.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist
structuralist.reasoning: Published scholarship does support reading Dulcinea as more than a mere initial fiction: critics repeatedly treat her as the organizing ideal of Don Quixote’s identity and as a figure whose symbolic force persists through the novel’s end, especially in relation to renunciation, repentance, and the collapse of knight-errantry. That said, the axis slightly overstates her as a fully developed “final moral center” in a psychological sense; scholarship more often frames her as an enduring imaginative and ethical reference point than as an independently dramatized endpoint of mutual intimacy.

psychological.label: Psychological Critic

Psychoanalytic and gender-oriented readings also stress that the relationship is less a conventional romance than a sustaining fantasy that organizes his ego, desire, and ethical self-understanding across the novel.

relational_axes.axis_name: From honored guest to manipulated spectacle
relational_axes.pole_start: He initially experiences the duke and duchess as noble patrons who recognize and elevate his knightly identity.
relational_axes.pole_end: He ends as a guest who still receives courtesy, but who increasingly understands, at least dimly, that their hospitality is also theatrical manipulation and mockery.

trajectory.position_description: The duke and duchess stage elaborate honors that make Don Quixote feel authentically knightly and socially visible.
key_moments: Ceremonial reception at the castle
Public honors and deference
Don Quixote feels truly recognized

trajectory.position_description: Their hospitality becomes increasingly prankish: Sancho is mocked, Altisidora is staged, and Don Quixote is repeatedly made part of a comic performance.
key_moments: Pranks on Sancho
Altisidora's mock love
Clavileño and other staged marvels

trajectory.position_description: He remains courteous, but the courtly environment now feels more conditional and cruel. He is humiliated, confined, and increasingly aware that noble hospitality can mask exploitation.
key_moments: Doña Rodriguez episode
Public humiliation and confinement
Departure from the castle after defeat

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This relationship is not a simple betrayal arc; it is a shift from sincere-seeming honor to elaborate social theater. Don Quixote remains deferential, but the emotional tone moves from validation to wary endurance.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist
structuralist.reasoning: This axis is well grounded in scholarship on the Duke and Duchess episodes as a sustained scene of aristocratic manipulation: critics regularly read the pair as staging Don Quixote’s knighthood for their own amusement. The proposed arc is also plausible narratologically, since the novel lets Don Quixote begin by accepting their patronage as recognition and later register, however dimly, that their courtesy is theatrical and mocking rather than genuinely honorific.

relational_axes.axis_name: From household ally to corrective opponent and back to partial reconciliation
relational_axes.pole_start: He begins with the curate as a familiar village authority, not yet an enemy, though already outside his fantasy world.
relational_axes.pole_end: He ends with a more cordial, socially integrated relation, even though the curate remains a manager of his sanity and narrative.

trajectory.position_description: The curate is still part of the household circle, but his role shifts sharply when he helps burn the books and diagnose Don Quixote's madness.

trajectory.position_description: By the end, the curate is again a trusted village figure. Don Quixote greets him affectionately and accepts his care, even as he renounces the old fantasy life.

Accepts advice and care
Dies reconciled within the household

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The curate's relationship with Don Quixote moves from domestic familiarity to corrective antagonism and then to a softened, reintegrated ending. He is one of the main external forces trying to cure him, but the final chapters restore social trust.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist

Structuralist and narratological readings often treat the curate not as a static antagonist but as part of the novel’s shifting regime of mediation, where he moves between neighborly familiarity, disciplinary opposition, and partial accommodation by the end. The proposed arc from familiar authority to corrective opponent and back to a more integrated relation is therefore defensible.
